Unbundling Multimodal Vision Encoding

Ellis Brown Affiliation: New York University    Chris Hoang Affiliation: New York University   
Shengyi Qian    Shang-Wen Li    Mike Lewis    Marjan Ghazvininejad    Luke Zettlemoyer    Lucas Beyer   
Mengye Ren Affiliation: New York University    Jakob Verbeek    Saining Xie Affiliation: New York University    Hu Xu Affiliation: Meta FAIR
Abstract

How multimodal language models should encode visual input remains up for debate. Most models use a pretrained vision encoder, while some recent recipes train the encoder from scratch with the language model or remove it entirely. Vision encoders bundle together three design choices: a visual prior from upstream pretraining, dedicated vision capacity, and pre-fusion placement of that capacity (i.e., before the multimodal backbone). Because published models also differ in data, architecture, and compute, comparing them cannot isolate the effect of each choice. We disentangle these choices via a controlled framework where we pretrain all models from scratch on common data and compare them on visual question answering and language benchmarks at matched lifetime compute. We find that the visual prior is not necessary; an encoder trained jointly from scratch is on par with a pretrained one, without a separate training stage. What matters instead is dedicated vision capacity: an encoder-free model trails on visual understanding even when its backbone is enlarged by the encoder’s parameter count. Yet that capacity need not precede multimodal fusion, as vision-only modules added in-fusion to early backbone layers perform comparably to a pre-fusion encoder and can lower time to first token. These results also hold across backbone sizes, when encoder pretraining is treated as free, and when starting from a pretrained language model. Overall, our findings favor dedicated vision capacity trained jointly with the backbone and placed early within it.

1 Introduction

Most multimodal models acquire visual understanding from a vision encoder pretrained for a separate objective, such as image recognition or image–text alignment, rather than from being trained directly with the multimodal backbone that uses its features (He et al., 2016; Radford et al., 2021; Tschannen et al., 2025; Siméoni et al., 2026; Tschannen et al., 2023). Multimodal training has progressed from freezing this encoder (Alayrac et al., 2022; Li et al., 2023b; Liu et al., 2023; Muse Glimmer Team, 2026) to updating it (Beyer et al., 2024; Bai et al., 2025a), but encoder pretraining has remained a separate stage. Recent recipes bring vision and language closer by discarding parts of the pretrained encoder setup: Kimi K3 trains a vision encoder from scratch jointly with the multimodal backbone (Kimi Team, 2026b), and encoder-free models directly process pixel patches, forcing visual encoding to be learned entirely within the backbone (Adept AI, 2023; Diao et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2026; Gemma Team, 2026; Thinking Machines Lab, 2026a). Each recipe implies a different answer to what the vision encoder contributes, if anything at all. We ask which of its inherited design choices benefit multimodal models trained entirely from scratch.

The predominant multimodal vision encoding recipes bundle together three design choices: (i) a visual prior from upstream pretraining, (ii) dedicated vision capacity (i.e., parameters that only vision tokens use), and (iii) pre-fusion placement of that capacity in a separate encoder that operates before vision and text tokens interact in the backbone—rather than operating in-fusion, within the shared backbone. A pretrained encoder keeps all three, a from-scratch encoder gives up only the prior, and an encoder-free model gives up all three.

Existing comparisons cannot isolate these choices, for two reasons. First, they entangle the choices with each other and the rest of the recipe. Published models differ in data, training stages, compute, and architecture. While controlled studies hold multimodal training data and compute fixed, their comparisons among pretrained encoders (McKinzie et al., 2024; Tong et al., 2024a; Fan et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025) vary which visual prior an encoder imports rather than whether it needs one in the first place. Studies of encoder-based vs. encoder-free models either change all three choices (Tong et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026) or change capacity and placement together (Shukor et al., 2025). Second, comparisons with pretrained encoders control only multimodal training, treating encoder pretraining as free even though it adds substantial compute and data of its own (e.g., SigLIP 2 trains on 40B image–text samples; Tschannen et al., 2025), and several studies attribute the encoder’s advantage to its pretraining (Lei et al., 2025; Diao et al., 2025).

In this work, we conduct a controlled study that unbundles the design choices of multimodal vision encoding one at a time (fig. 1): (i) does the vision encoder need separate pretraining? (ii) does vision encoding need dedicated capacity? and (iii) does that capacity need to precede multimodal fusion? We train every model entirely from scratch, language backbone included, on a common pool of data with one encoder architecture, one dense backbone architecture, and one optimization recipe. We evaluate models on downstream visual question-answering (VQA) and language benchmarks at backbone sizes from 0.6B to 6.4B. Because recipes spend compute in different stages, we compare them at matched lifetime compute: the total compute of all training stages, including any pretraining of the encoder or language model.

Our experiments answer these questions and test whether the answers hold beyond lifetime compute:

  1. 1.

    Separate pretraining is optional (§3). At matched lifetime compute, a from-scratch encoder is on par with encoders pretrained on the same data. Even if we ignore upstream compute (§6.1), more encoder pretraining improves recognition but not VQA.

  2. 2.

    Dedicated vision capacity is key (§4). An encoder-free model trails an encoder-based model on visual understanding, even when its backbone is enlarged by the encoder’s parameter count. The encoder’s advantage thus lies in capacity dedicated to vision rather than in total parameter count.

  3. 3.

    Vision capacity can move in-fusion (§5). Adding vision-only capacity to the backbone’s earliest layers is comparable to adding a from-scratch pre-fusion encoder. Scaling laws show in-fusion tracking the encoder, whereas encoder-free trails it at every size (§5.4).

  4. 4.

    The findings hold beyond lifetime compute (§6). Starting from a pretrained 1.7B language model, in-fusion stays comparable to the from-scratch encoder while encoder-free falls further behind. In-fusion can also lower time to first token, since no separate encoder must run before the backbone.

Together, these findings show that multimodal models benefit from dedicated vision capacity, which however needs neither separate pretraining nor pre-fusion placement.

2 A controlled protocol for comparing multimodal recipes

We propose a protocol that varies the three design choices a vision encoder bundles, while holding fixed the data sources, optimization settings, compute, and backbone architecture. This isolates their effects when comparing current multimodal model recipes. Conclusions about these design choices cannot be drawn from comparing published models, because they differ in several factors at once—e.g., they build on different pretrained language models and vision encoders that each vary in training data and compute. We therefore use no external pretrained models: we train every component from scratch, with common data sources and training setups, and compare recipes at matched lifetime compute, the total compute of all training stages.

2.1 Recipes and the fusion boundary

All recipes differ only in how they encode visual input.

Backbone.

Our backbones use an architecture modeled after Qwen3 (Yang et al., 2025): a dense, decoder-only, pre-norm Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017) with RMSNorm (Zhang and Sennrich, 2019), RoPE (Su et al., 2024), SwiGLU feed-forward layers (Shazeer, 2020), and grouped-query attention (Ainslie et al., 2023) with query–key normalization (Dehghani et al., 2023) (section A.1). Our main comparisons (sections 3, 4 and 5) use the Qwen3 1.7B and 4B configurations with dedicated vision capacity fixed at 0.4B parameters, and our scaling study (section 5.4) uses a 0.6B–6.4B ladder that grows vision capacity in proportion to the backbone. Training uses autoregressive cross-entropy on text tokens; vision tokens precede the text they condition and have no loss. Each image’s vision tokens attend to each other bidirectionally and text tokens attend causally to all earlier tokens, including vision tokens (section A.4).

Fusion boundary.

We describe how image patches reach the backbone relative to the multimodal fusion boundary, the first layer in which vision and text tokens can interact: vision-only computation before it is pre-fusion and computation inside the shared backbone is in-fusion (figs. 1 and 1). Scratch encoders () process image patches pre-fusion with a randomly initialized 27-layer, 0.4B-parameter Vision Transformer (Dosovitskiy et al., 2021; Alabdulmohsin et al., 2023) modeled after MoonViT-V2 (Kimi K3’s encoder; Kimi Team, 2026b), whose output is linearly projected into the backbone. Pretrained encoders () share this architecture, but we first pretrain them ourselves on our common data (section 2.2) rather than taking external checkpoints. Encoder-free models () map patches directly into the backbone with a linear patch embedding (Adept AI, 2023; Gemma Team, 2026), followed by RMSNorm and a learned scalar gate (Qi et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026). In-fusion models () instead add vision-only modules inside the backbone (section 5). Every recipe trains on 224×224224\times 224 images, read as 256 vision tokens using 14×1414\times 14 patches. Instruction tuning for evaluation raises the resolution to 448×448448\times 448 (1,024 vision tokens), as in PaliGemma’s short high-resolution stage (Beyer et al., 2024), since OCR and chart reading needs fine detail (Tong et al., 2024a; Beyer, 2024).

2.2 Common data

Text-only sequences come from Nemotron-CC v2/v2.1 (NVIDIA, 2025b; NVIDIA, 2025a), and image–text sequences use MetaCLIP 1.2 pairs (English subset) (Xu et al., 2024). Encoder pretraining uses these pairs with their original alt-text, as in each objective’s original setup (section 3; e.g., CapPa, Tschannen et al., 2023), while multimodal training uses captions regenerated by Qwen2.5-VL-32B (Bai et al., 2025b) and shared by every recipe. Multimodal training mixes text-only and image–text sequences 70:30, so recipes with a pretrained encoder spend more lifetime compute on image–text data. This matches the language share Han et al. (2026) found optimal and gave the best visual understanding in our sweep at a small cost to text (section A.4).

2.3 Lifetime compute

Multimodal models often build on separately pretrained components whose training can even exceed the multimodal stage. For example, SigLIP 2, a commonly used encoder, is trained on 40B image–text samples (Tschannen et al., 2025), which translates to 10 trillion image tokens, while language models are typically also trained on trillions of text tokens (Touvron et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2025). Counting only multimodal training therefore favors recipes that spend more compute in these earlier stages. To make such comparisons fair, we propose lifetime compute, the total training compute of every stage that produces the final model,

Clifetime=∑s∈𝒮Cs,C_{\mathrm{lifetime}}=\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}}C_{s}, (1)

where 𝒮\mathcal{S} is the set of training stages and CsC_{s} is the training compute of stage ss. Here, 𝒮\mathcal{S} contains multimodal training, any text-only training before it and, for pretrained encoders, encoder pretraining, but not instruction tuning. We report compute in FLOPs; because recipes differ in cost per token, matched compute means that they process different numbers of tokens. Section A.5 describes the compute accounting and converts each budget into token-equivalents, the number of tokens a text-only model of the same size would process with the same compute. Lifetime compute models a project that allocates one budget across every training stage, which lets us separate the contribution of each design choice. In practice, pretrained encoders are often available for free, so we also compare encoders with their pretraining compute not counted (section 6.1).

2.4 Training schedule

To compare recipes at many training lengths from one run (Zhai et al., 2022), we use a warmup–stable–decay schedule (Hu et al., 2024; Wen et al., 2025; Hägele et al., 2024), where the learning rate stays constant after warmup and any checkpoint of that run can be decayed to 5% of its peak over the final 10% of training (section A.3). Our main comparisons span compute budgets from 6.5×10206.5\times 10^{20} to 2.9×10222.9\times 10^{22} FLOPs, or 56B to 1.11T token-equivalents (table 12). We index budgets by tokens per parameter (TPP): token-equivalents divided by the backbone’s non-embedding parameters, i.e., all parameters except the tied token embedding (1.4B at 1.7B and 3.6B at 4B; backbones are named by their total parameters). Budgets reach 788 TPP at 1.7B and 306 TPP at 4B. All recipes share one peak learning rate per backbone size, scaled with the inverse square root of its total parameter count (3×10−43\times 10^{-4} at 1.7B and 2×10−42\times 10^{-4} at 4B). At 1.7B, the encoder’s lead over encoder-free and parity with in-fusion hold from half to twice that learning rate (section F.2).

2.5 Evaluation

We evaluate recipes on text and visual understanding benchmarks and report the following metrics. Avg. Text averages four category means over 12 language benchmarks: commonsense reasoning (COPA, HellaSwag, PIQA, Social IQa, and WinoGrande (Roemmele et al., 2011; Zellers et al., 2019; Bisk et al., 2020; Sap et al., 2019; Sakaguchi et al., 2020)), science question answering (ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge, and OpenBookQA (Clark et al., 2018; Mihaylov et al., 2018)), broad knowledge (MMLU (Hendrycks et al., 2021)), and reading comprehension (RACE-middle, RACE-high, and BoolQ (Lai et al., 2017; Clark et al., 2019)). Avg. VQA averages the general, knowledge, OCR and chart, and vision-centric category means of the 16 Cambrian visual question-answering benchmarks (Tong et al., 2024a), after instruction tuning each checkpoint for three epochs on Cambrian-7M with 448×448448\times 448 images. A text-only model at the same lifetime compute serves as a reference for Avg. Text (section B.3). Sections 4 and 5.4 also compare held-out caption loss on images never seen in training (section B.4). Appendix B details the benchmarks, and appendix I gives every benchmark score.

3 Does the vision encoder need separate pretraining?

The first design choice a vision encoder bundles is a visual prior imported through separate pretraining, which recent models (Kimi Team, 2026b) forgo by training the encoder from scratch with the language model. Under a fixed lifetime compute budget, encoder pretraining directly competes with multimodal training for FLOPs. Whether the prior is needed also shapes the remainder of our study, because encoder-free architectures cannot easily import one. We test whether the prior helps by comparing encoders pretrained with different objectives against the same encoder trained from scratch with the backbone.

Setup.

We pretrain a separate encoder with each of four objectives and the same compute: contrastive image–text alignment (MetaCLIP; Xu et al., 2024), self-supervised learning (WebSSL; Fan et al., 2025), and captioning (Cap and CapPa; Tschannen et al., 2023). Pretrained encoders are updated during multimodal training and compared with an encoder trained from scratch at matched lifetime compute; we also test a frozen MetaCLIP encoder. MetaCLIP, an instance of widely used CLIP-style pretraining (Radford et al., 2021; Zhai et al., 2023; Tschannen et al., 2025), serves as the pretrained reference in the remaining experiments. Section C.1 details the pretraining objectives and section A.1 the encoder architecture.

A from-scratch encoder is on par with pretrained ones.

With a 1.7B backbone and a 1.04×10221.04\times 10^{22} FLOP budget, all four pretrained encoders are comparable to the from-scratch encoder when pretraining takes 7.4% or 15% of the budget (e.g., Cap sees 1B or 2B image–text examples). Larger upstream shares hurt multimodal performance: at a 60% share, both averages fall clearly below the from-scratch encoder (fig. 2). Across backbone sizes, the from-scratch encoder matches or exceeds MetaCLIP at every budget (fig. 2). Appendix C gives the per-objective results, including frozen encoders, the full pretraining sweep, the results at 4B, and compositional image–text matching on SugarCrepe (Hsieh et al., 2023).

Encoder pretraining does not help even when its compute is free (section 6.1). More pretraining raises ImageNet accuracy but not Avg. VQA, and pretrained encoders are only comparable to the from-scratch encoder at matched multimodal compute. Delaying vision also hurts, as training on text alone for the first 25–75% of training, with the total number of image–text examples held fixed, clearly lowers Avg. VQA (table 11), consistent with the vision laziness that Han et al. (2026) observe after text-only training.

4 Does vision encoding need dedicated capacity?

The from-scratch encoder of section 3 forgoes the imported prior but keeps the second design choice: dedicated vision capacity. Encoder-free models drop this capacity entirely and project image patches directly into the shared backbone (Adept AI, 2023; Diao et al., 2024; Liu et al., 2026; Gemma Team, 2026; Thinking Machines Lab, 2026a). Dropping the encoder, however, also removes a substantial number of parameters and changes how raw patches enter the backbone, so a gap between the two recipes could reflect fewer total parameters, a weak patch embedding, or missing dedicated capacity. In this section, we test whether visual understanding needs this dedicated capacity, leaving the study of its precise placement to section 5.

Setup.

We compare the from-scratch encoder (section 3) with the encoder-free recipe (section 2.1), which maps each patch into the backbone with a linear patch embedding followed by RMSNorm and a learned gate. As in every recipe, vision tokens attend to one another bidirectionally in the backbone (section 2.1). Both recipes share common backbones, data, and lifetime compute budgets, and we compare them at 1.7B and 4B.

Encoder-free trails encoder on visual understanding.

Figure 3 shows that Avg. VQA clearly suffers from a missing encoder, across scales and budgets, while Avg. Text stays comparable. This also holds when scaling the encoder’s size (section 5.4). This result differs from Shukor et al. (2025), who find that encoder-free models match or slightly outperform encoder-based ones, mainly at smaller sizes. We identify two choices in their setup that work against the encoder (section D.4). First, their encoder’s learning rate may have been too small. Second, they fit their scaling laws to an average of text, interleaved, and caption losses, which drowns out the signal from vision. In-distribution held-out caption loss instead shows the encoder-free deficit and tracks Avg. VQA across recipes, sizes, and budgets (fig. 18), whereas their averaged loss hides it.

Matching total parameters does not overcome encoder-free’s deficit.

We next widen or deepen the encoder-free backbone by 0.4B parameters to match the vision parameters added by the encoder (table 2; 4B in table 19). None of the variants comes close to closing the gap on Avg. VQA, though all improve Avg. Text, since text tokens also use the added parameters. The remaining gap in visual understanding is largest on OCR and chart benchmarks. The same parameters are thus more useful as a vision encoder. As none of these variants improves Avg. VQA, encoder-free hereafter keeps the plain backbone shared across all recipes.

A richer patch embedding does not close the gap.

We also study replacing the encoder-free linear patch embedding with two richer ones: a normalized two-layer projection inspired by Gemma 4 (Gemma Team, 2026), and a four-layer hierarchical MLP (Touvron et al., 2022), as in Inkling (Thinking Machines Lab, 2026a). Trained on 224×224224\times 224 images, neither comes close to the encoder (table 2), though the hierarchical MLP matches it when compressing 640×640640\times 640 images into the same 256 tokens (section D.3). Subsequent encoder-free experiments keep the default patch embedding, so dedicated capacity is placed deliberately.

5 Does dedicated capacity need to precede multimodal fusion?

Section 4 shows that visual understanding benefits from dedicated capacity. We now ask whether that capacity must precede multimodal fusion. The encoder’s parameters are both dedicated, used only by vision tokens, and pre-fusion, processing vision tokens before they interact with text. We test whether pre-fusion placement is needed by moving the encoder’s parameter budget in-fusion, into vision-only modules inside the shared backbone (section 5.1). Section 5.2 studies where this capacity should sit, which tokens should use it, and which modules it adds. Sections 5.3 and 5.4 then compare it with the encoder over training and with scale.

5.1 Moving the encoder’s capacity inside the backbone

In-fusion vision capacity adds vision-only modules to selected backbone layers. In each of these layers, the attention projections and the feed-forward network (FFN) keep their shared weights and add vision-only counterparts, whose outputs add to the shared outputs after each module (fig. 4). Each vision-only module thus acts as an additive expert routed by modality: vision tokens use it alongside the shared weights. Unlike mixture-of-transformers (Liang et al., 2025, MoT;), which gives text and vision tokens entirely separate parameters, in-fusion still passes every token through the shared parameters. Section 6.2 compares the two when starting from pretrained language models.

For token ii with vision indicator mi∈{0,1}m_{i}\in\{0,1\}, each attention projection WPW_{P} gains a vision-only counterpart Δ​WP\Delta W_{P} that applies only to vision tokens,

P⁡(𝐳i)=WP​𝐳i+mi​Δ​WP​𝐳i,P∈{Q,K,V,O},P(\mathbf{z}_{i})=W_{P}\,\mathbf{z}_{i}+m_{i}\,\Delta W_{P}\,\mathbf{z}_{i},\qquad P\in\{Q,K,V,O\}, (2)

where 𝐳i\mathbf{z}_{i} is the projection’s input (the normalized hidden state for QQ, KK, VV and the attention output for OO). Attention thus remains joint across vision and text tokens. The FFN gains a vision-only branch,

𝐡i′=𝐡i+F⁡(N⁡(𝐡i))+mi​Δ​F​(N⁡(𝐡i)),\mathbf{h}_{i}^{\prime}=\mathbf{h}_{i}+F\!\left(N(\mathbf{h}_{i})\right)+m_{i}\,\Delta F\!\left(N(\mathbf{h}_{i})\right), (3)

where FF is the shared FFN, NN is its normalization, and Δ​F\Delta F is a vision-only FFN of the same form that reads the same normalized input (section E.1). The vision-only projections Δ​WP\Delta W_{P} and the output projection of Δ​F\Delta F are zero-initialized, so training starts from the shared model. Because these modules act only when mi=1m_{i}=1, text-only inputs are processed exactly as they would have been by the shared backbone.

We use two variants: “in-fusion”, our default, adds vision FFN branches of smaller hidden width and vision-only counterparts of all four attention projections, while “in-fusion (FFN-only)” adds only vision FFN branches. We size both variants to match the encoder’s vision-only parameter budget (table 23), so comparisons with the encoder vary only where dedicated capacity is placed. Existing vision-specific architectures do not fit this comparison: they either duplicate vision weights that scale with the backbone (Wang et al., 2024; Liang et al., 2025) or use vision adapters that rely on an encoder (Dong et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025).

5.2 Where and how to add in-fusion capacity

We compare in-fusion designs that reallocate the encoder’s 0.4B vision parameters within the backbone.

Placement of capacity within fusion.

We study placement with the FFN-only variant, because FFN branches can be narrowed to fit any placement. Full-rank vision-only attention projections cannot, because adding them to every layer would take 88% of the 0.4B budget at 1.7B and exceed it at 4B. With the budget fixed, we compare four placements (table 3): a narrow branch in every layer, or eight wider branches spread evenly across depth, in the last eight layers, or in the first eight layers. The first three variants do no better than the encoder-free model on Avg. VQA, whereas placing the modules in the first eight layers matches the scratch encoder. Early placement also helps most on OCR and chart questions, which depend on fine visual detail, whereas late placement does not. Dedicated in-fusion capacity is therefore most useful where the backbone first processes vision tokens, similar to an encoder. We hypothesize that vision tokens benefit most from vision-only processing while they are still close to raw patch features. Only early placement concentrates the budget there, whereas the every-layer and spread placements dilute it across the backbone. Layerwise representation similarity shows that the in-fusion models change vision tokens mostly within the first eight blocks, where their vision-only modules sit, and little afterward, while the encoder-free model keeps changing them through shared blocks 4–13 (section E.4). Therefore, we use the first eight layers from here on.

Reserving the capacity for vision tokens matters.

To check that the gain comes from reserving this capacity for vision tokens, we also give the same parameters in the first eight layers to all tokens (table 3). Widening the shared FFNs barely improves over the encoder-free model. A separate branch used by all tokens recovers some of the vision-only branch’s gain, but still trails it even with twice the training (table 24). The all-token variants slightly improve on Avg. Text, because text also uses the added parameters. We hypothesize that a vision-only branch gives vision tokens processing of their own without competing with text for the same parameters, while both still share the backbone’s attention and FFNs.

Adding vision-only attention projections.

With the capacity confined to the first eight layers, the QKVO attention projections fit within the budget (0.1B at 1.7B), so “in-fusion” adds them alongside narrower FFN branches. It is comparable to FFN-only at 1.7B and slightly ahead at every 4B budget (fig. 5), and its vision-only attention projections help on their own at 4B (section E.2), so we use this variant as our default for the remainder of the paper.

5.3 Can in-fusion capacity match a pre-fusion encoder?

With the same dedicated budget on either side of the multimodal fusion boundary, we compare in-fusion with a scratch encoder at matched lifetime compute over training at 1.7B and 4B (fig. 6). In-fusion is comparable to the encoder throughout. Like the encoder, in-fusion clearly leads encoder-free at both sizes; section 5.4 compares the recipes across backbone sizes. Part of the in-fusion budget sits in vision-only attention projections, which help on their own in additional 4B ablations (section E.2). Dedicated vision capacity therefore does not need to precede fusion to benefit visual understanding. In-fusion can also lower time to first token for image requests, since no encoder runs before the backbone (section 6.3).

5.4 Results hold with scale

So far, we have compared the recipes at 1.7B and 4B with 0.4B of dedicated vision capacity. To see how they behave with scale, we train them on a ladder of five backbone sizes from 0.6B to 6.4B (setup in appendix G). The dedicated vision capacity grows with the backbone, keeping its share of parameters from the 1.7B model, as in jointly scaled models (Chen et al., 2023; Tian et al., 2025). For each recipe, we fit Avg. VQA, caption loss, and text loss as functions of model size NN and token-equivalents DD on all of its ladder runs. At every size, encoder-free needs approximately three times the encoder’s compute to match it on Avg. VQA and caption loss, while in-fusion tracks the encoder (fig. 7). On text loss and Avg. Text, the three recipes are comparable (tables 30 and 29). Taken together, the findings of sections 4 and 5 hold with scale.

6 Vision encoding beyond lifetime compute

Our main investigations (sections 3, 4 and 5) are deliberately controlled: they train every component from scratch and charge each stage’s compute to one lifetime budget, which enables us to isolate the three design choices of a vision encoder. In practice, however, multimodal models are often built from separately pretrained components: a language model and, usually, a vision encoder. Inference speed for serving also shapes these design decisions. We find that a “free” pretrained encoder still does not help a backbone trained from scratch (section 6.1), and that instead midtraining a 1.7B text-only model leaves the comparisons of sections 3, 4 and 5 unchanged (section 6.2). Finally, in-fusion can lower the time to first token for image requests (section 6.3).

6.1 Zero-cost pretrained encoders

Section 3 charges encoder pretraining to the lifetime budget, but in practice a pretrained encoder is often available for free. Here, we hold multimodal training fixed at 2.7×10212.7\times 10^{21} FLOPs and vary MetaCLIP pretraining from 1.4×10211.4\times 10^{21} to 9.0×10219.0\times 10^{21} FLOPs. This raises the encoder’s ImageNet linear-probe accuracy before multimodal training from 80.4% to 84.4% (fig. 9; section C.3), yet Avg. VQA is highest after the shortest pretraining, and an encoder trained from scratch with the same multimodal training matches it. Thus, even when pretraining is free, more of it does not help.

6.2 Midtraining from pretrained language models

Many multimodal models add vision to a language model pretrained on text alone (Alayrac et al., 2022; Liu et al., 2023; Tong et al., 2024a; Bai et al., 2025a). We call this stage of continued training on multimodal data midtraining. We test whether the comparisons of sections 3, 4 and 5 hold in this setting. We pretrain our own 1.7B language model on 1T tokens of the same text data and then midtrain it to 1.33T token-equivalents with each recipe at equal compute (fig. 9). Following DeepSeek-VL (Lu et al., 2024a), midtraining keeps 70% text data; as in section 6.1, MetaCLIP’s encoder pretraining is not counted. Besides the four recipes, we compare MoT (section 5.1, initialized from the language model) and a variant that copies only its first eight layers, matching the encoder’s 0.4B vision-only parameters.

In-fusion, MoT layers 1–8, and the from-scratch encoder perform comparably, and all lead encoder-free. The full MoT model falls behind despite 3.5 times as many vision-only parameters—adding vision-only copies of the later layers to MoT layers 1–8 hurts, consistent with late placement not helping in section 5.2. A free MetaCLIP encoder, which matches the from-scratch encoder when the backbone is also trained from scratch (section 6.1), trails it here, mostly on OCR, chart, and vision-centric questions. Tuning each encoder’s learning rate does not change these conclusions (section H.1). We hypothesize that the from-scratch encoder learns features suited to the pretrained language model from its first update, whereas MetaCLIP’s contrastive features, which miss fine visual detail (Tong et al., 2024b), must be reshaped by a language model that already leans on text. Every recipe keeps Avg. Text within a point of a text-only control. Thus, the conclusions from our controlled experiments (sections 3, 4 and 5) carry over to midtraining, where a free pretrained encoder trails the from-scratch encoder, encoder-free trails on VQA, and in-fusion is comparable to the pre-fusion encoder.

6.3 Training and inference speed

A separate encoder must finish processing each image before the backbone can start, which adds a serial step to inference. Following the inference benchmark of Mono-InternVL (Luo et al., 2025b), we measure time to first token (TTFT) on one H200 with 16 concurrent requests, each with one 448-pixel image and 256 text tokens (section H.3). At 1.7B with 0.4B vision-only parameters, in-fusion and its FFN-only variant are clearly faster than the encoder (fig. 10) at comparable Avg. VQA (table 26). MoT, which copies the first kk backbone layers for vision tokens, is about as fast as in-fusion up to 0.4B vision-only parameters, but its added TTFT grows faster with the budget, while staying below the encoder’s TTFT. Encoder-free is fastest but clearly trails on Avg. VQA (table 26). In-fusion’s TTFT advantage over the encoder grows with the vision-only budget (fig. 10), which scales with the backbone (section 5.4); at a fixed budget, vision adds nearly the same time at 1.7B and 4B (table 36). Earlier encoder-free models report larger TTFT reductions, up to 69% (Luo et al., 2025b; Luo et al., 2025a), although their gains also reflect other efficiency changes. Inference benefits also depend on deployment details. Under continuous batching of mixed text and image requests, in-fusion’s vision-only modules run in the same forward passes as text-only requests, whereas a separate encoder adds latency only to image requests. Finally, both in-fusion variants train as fast as encoder-free, whereas the encoder recipe is 3% slower at 4B (table 35).

7 Related work

Multimodal model recipes.

Most multimodal models connect a separately pretrained vision encoder (Radford et al., 2021; Tschannen et al., 2025; Bolya et al., 2025), kept frozen (Liu et al., 2023; Li et al., 2023b; Muse Glimmer Team, 2026) or updated (Beyer et al., 2024; Steiner et al., 2024; Bai et al., 2025a), to a pretrained language model. More recent models train the encoder from scratch with the language model (Kimi Team, 2026b; Tian et al., 2025), embed image patches without an encoder (Adept AI, 2023; Diao et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026; Gemma Team, 2026; Thinking Machines Lab, 2026a), or quantize images with a separately trained tokenizer (Chameleon Team, 2024; Wang et al., 2026). Inkling was released as “encoder-free”, yet its successor, Inkling 2 Small, uses a 292M-parameter vision encoder (Thinking Machines Lab, 2026a; Thinking Machines Lab, 2026b). Because these models also differ in data, pretrained components, and compute, comparing them directly does not isolate a single design choice. We therefore train every stage of each recipe class from scratch on common data sources and compare the recipes at matched lifetime compute (section 2).

Controlled studies.

Prior controlled studies of encoder pretraining typically start from a pretrained language model, count only multimodal training, and compare encoder pretraining objectives and data (Karamcheti et al., 2024; McKinzie et al., 2024; Tong et al., 2024a; Laurençon et al., 2024; Fan et al., 2025; Li et al., 2025) rather than studying whether separate pretraining is needed at all. The few works that compare pretrained and from-scratch encoders vary in their findings, possibly because they control neither the encoder’s pretraining data nor lifetime compute (Tian et al., 2025; Kimi Team, 2026b). Studies raise a similar question for language pretraining, finding that adding vision before text-only pretraining ends, rather than after it, improves visual understanding (Keh et al., 2025; Han et al., 2026; Kimi Team, 2026a), as in our delayed-vision experiments (table 11). Encoder pretraining also confounds encoder vs. encoder-free comparisons, which typically pit a pretrained encoder against an encoder-free model (Beyer et al., 2024; Diao et al., 2024; Lei et al., 2025; Diao et al., 2025; Tong et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2026; Chen et al., 2026). Such comparisons remove separate pretraining, dedicated capacity, and pre-fusion placement at once, and often attribute the encoder’s advantage to pretraining data they do not control. Shukor et al. (2025), who train both designs from scratch, find that encoder-free models match or slightly outperform an encoder. In contrast, we find that the encoder leads on VQA and held-out caption loss, which we trace to their setup (section D.4).

Dedicated vision capacity.

Testing whether dedicated capacity must precede fusion requires moving the encoder’s capacity inside the backbone, which the encoder vs. encoder-free comparisons cannot accomplish. Prior works on fusion depth come closer, varying where modalities begin to interact (Nagrani et al., 2021; Hao et al., 2026) or where encoder features enter the backbone (Meng et al., 2024), but none moves a fixed amount of vision-only capacity into layers that vision and text share. Other multimodal architectures add vision-specific parameters to the backbone, but not in a form that fits this comparison. Modality-expert designs duplicate the backbone’s weights for vision tokens, typically in every layer, and route vision tokens through these copies instead of the shared weights (Bao et al., 2022; Lin et al., 2024; Liang et al., 2025). Their vision-only capacity is thus set by the backbone’s size and spread over its depth rather than held at an encoder’s budget early in the model, and most also build on a pretrained language model (Wang et al., 2024; Luo et al., 2025b; Tian et al., 2025; Diao et al., 2025; Shi et al., 2025). Adapter architectures fine-tune a pretrained model through small parallel or low-rank modules shared by all tokens (He et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2022; Hu et al., 2022), and their multimodal variants keep an encoder alongside the adapters (Dong et al., 2024; Shapourian et al., 2026) or distill from one (Wang et al., 2025). The encoders in these works still supply pre-fusion capacity or a pretrained prior, the two factors our comparison aims to remove. We instead give vision tokens their own attention projections and feed-forward branches in selected backbone layers. Their outputs add to the shared ones and together match an encoder’s parameter budget, so only the placement of this capacity changes (section 5). Placed in the first eight layers, in-fusion capacity is comparable to a pre-fusion encoder on VQA, so dedicated vision capacity helps whether it sits pre-fusion or in-fusion.

8 Discussion

With multimodal models revisiting the vision encoder, we asked which of its design choices are still beneficial. We proposed unbundling the encoder into three choices: a visual prior from separate pretraining, dedicated vision capacity, and pre-fusion placement of that capacity. We tested each by training every recipe from scratch on common data, with one architecture and optimization setup, and comparing recipes on text and visual understanding benchmarks at matched lifetime compute.

Takeaways from unbundling.

Of the three choices an encoder bundles, only dedicated vision capacity maintains its advantage. Separate pretraining is unnecessary: an encoder trained jointly with the backbone is on par with pretrained ones, and longer pretraining improves recognition but not VQA, even when it is free (sections 3 and 6.1). Dedicated capacity matters: with the encoder’s parameters added to their shared backbone, encoder-free models gain on Avg. Text but still trail the encoder on Avg. VQA (section 4), most on OCR and chart questions (table 2). This capacity belongs early, but it need not precede the backbone: vision-only modules in the first backbone layers are comparable to a pre-fusion encoder (section 5). For recipes that drop the encoder, this suggests reallocating its parameters as vision-only capacity in the earliest layers rather than as shared parameters.

Limitations and future work.

To keep comparisons controlled, we pretrain encoders on the same images as multimodal training, so our results do not rule out a benefit from released encoders trained on additional data. Encoder pretraining uses the images’ original alt-text, as in standard image–text pretraining; pretraining on our regenerated captions instead changes little (table 9). Our experiments are on dense backbones with up to 6.4B parameters; the most compelling next step is extending them to sparse mixture-of-experts backbones, whose experts could naturally host in-fusion’s modality-routed capacity. Multimodal training also uses 224×224224\times 224 MetaCLIP images, leaving higher-resolution training and more text-rich data to future work. The text–image data mixture was selected with the from-scratch encoder at 1.7B, so mixtures tuned for each recipe remain underexplored (section A.4). Finally, how architecture interacts with interleaved image–text and video data remains open.

Conclusion.

We presented a controlled study that disentangles the design choices behind how multimodal models process visual input, studying each choice in isolation instead of as part of a bundled recipe. Rather than assembling multimodal models from components optimized for different objectives, our findings favor training them end-to-end as one system.
