Tables abbreviate the Avg. Text categories as Com (commonsense reasoning), Sci (science question answering), Knw (broad knowledge), and Rdg (reading comprehension), and the Avg. VQA categories as Gen (general), Knw (knowledge), OCR (OCR and chart), and Vis (vision-centric). appendix B defines them.

\FloatBarrier

Appendix A Controlled protocol

Unless stated otherwise, every comparison of the 1.7B and 4B backbones uses the settings below, which detail the protocol of section 2.

A.1 Architectures

The multimodal recipes differ in where their vision-only capacity sits and how it is trained: in a pre-fusion vision encoder that is pretrained and then frozen or updated, or trained from scratch, encoder-free with no module besides a patch embedding, or vision-only modules inside the shared backbone (in-fusion vision capacity; section E.1). Unless a variable is the stated ablation, comparisons hold the backbone, the 256 vision tokens per image in multimodal training, the data, the optimization recipe, and lifetime compute fixed. Table 4 lists the backbone and encoder architectures.

Backbone.

The shared backbone is a dense decoder-only Transformer that follows the Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-4B configurations (Yang et al., 2025) and is trained from random initialization. Its FFNs use SwiGLU (Shazeer, 2020), and its attention uses grouped key–value heads with RMSNorm on queries and keys. The vision-only FFN branches of in-fusion vision capacity use the same form and read the same normalized input as the shared FFN (section E.1).

Vision encoder.

The encoder follows MoonViT-V2, the vision encoder of Kimi K3 (Kimi Team, 2026b), in depth, patch size, normalization, and size: 27 layers, patch size 14, RMSNorm, and about 0.4B parameters in total. It has width 1,024 with 4,096-wide MLPs and uses learned spatial position embeddings combined with interleaved two-dimensional rotary position embeddings. During multimodal training, each image is resized bilinearly to a shorter side of 224 pixels, center-cropped to 224×224224\times 224, and divided into 14×1414\times 14 patches, producing 256 vision tokens. For an image xx, the encoder recipe computes

venc​(x)=Wproj​fϕ​(x),v_{\mathrm{enc}}(x)=W_{\mathrm{proj}}f_{\phi}(x), (4)

where fϕf_{\phi} is the vision encoder and the linear projector WprojW_{\mathrm{proj}} maps its output width to the backbone width. Pretrained variants (section 3) use the same architecture and differ only in the pretraining objective. MetaCLIP and WebSSL use a class token during upstream training; we discard it and pass only the 256 patch tokens to the backbone (Liu et al., 2023).

Encoder-free patch embedding.

The encoder-free recipe projects each flattened 14×1414\times 14 RGB patch linearly into the backbone width, as in Fuyu and Gemma 4 (Adept AI, 2023; Gemma Team, 2026), and applies RMSNorm and a learned scalar gate (Qi et al., 2026; Li et al., 2026), giving 256 backbone tokens per image:

vfree​(x)=g​RMSNorm⁡(Wpatch​Patchify⁡(x)+p2​D),v_{\mathrm{free}}(x)=g\,\operatorname{RMSNorm}\left(W_{\mathrm{patch}}\operatorname{Patchify}(x)+p_{2\mathrm{D}}\right), (5)

where p2​Dp_{2\mathrm{D}} is a fixed two-dimensional sine–cosine position embedding and the learned scalar gate gg is initialized to 0.10.1. The in-fusion models of section E.1 use the same patch embedding.

\FloatBarrier

A.2 Encoder design selection

We chose the from-scratch encoder’s shape and size at matched lifetime compute, and every main comparison uses the resulting 27-layer, 0.4B encoder. The shape and size comparisons use the 1.7B backbone at 2.6×10212.6\times 10^{21} FLOPs (table 5).

The configurations in table 5 vary the structure of the dedicated visual computation. Half-Depth, Wide, and Shallow + Wide are pre-fusion encoders that change the default encoder’s depth, width, or both. The backbone-style encoder is also a pre-fusion encoder. It has its own patch embedding and eight Transformer blocks shaped like those of the 1.7B backbone, and it connects to the backbone through the linear projection of eq. 4. The Default, Shallow + Wide, and backbone-style variants use about the same vision-only parameter budget; the Half-Depth and Wide variants test smaller and larger budgets, respectively. The “Size” section of table 5 scales the default encoder’s depth and width together, from Small (0.05B) to Huge (0.92B). At matched lifetime compute, encoders with more parameters process fewer tokens.

The default encoder is comparable to Wide on VQA while using fewer vision-only parameters. Avg. Text does not follow encoder size: Small and Huge score highest, and the default slightly lower.

At 4B.

We further ablate encoder size at the 4B model scale, using the same from-scratch recipe (table 6). The default Large encoder is strongest on both Avg. Text and Avg. VQA. At both scales, the default encoder gives the highest Avg. VQA, and Avg. Text does not follow encoder size.

At 6.4B.

On the 6.4B backbone of the size ladder (appendix G), we also keep the 0.4B encoder instead of scaling it to 1.7B with the backbone. It is comparable to the scaled encoder on both averages at every budget (table 7), so the default encoder does not limit the encoder recipe at larger backbones either.

\FloatBarrier

A.3 Optimization settings

Table 8 lists the optimization settings for multimodal training and instruction tuning. We train the Transformer weight matrices with Muon (Jordan et al., 2024), applied per head to the query, key, and value projections (Kimi Team, 2026b), and the embeddings, output heads, normalization parameters, and biases with AdamW. The peak learning rate scales with the inverse square root of the backbone’s total parameter count, and training follows a warmup–stable–decay schedule (Hu et al., 2024; Wen et al., 2025; Hägele et al., 2024). Checkpoints taken before the final decay use a constant learning rate. The decay lowers the learning rate linearly to 5% of its peak over the last 10% of updates, so a run whose stable phase ends at compute CC finishes at C/0.9C/0.9 (for example, 1.17×10221.17\times 10^{22} and 1.30×10221.30\times 10^{22} FLOPs at 1.7B and 2.61×10222.61\times 10^{22} and 2.90×10222.90\times 10^{22} FLOPs at 4B; table 12).

\FloatBarrier

A.4 Training data and mixture

Text-only sequences come from Nemotron-CC v2 (NVIDIA, 2025b) and v2.1 (NVIDIA, 2025a), and image–text sequences use MetaCLIP 1.2 image–text pairs (English subset) (Xu et al., 2024). Every training sequence has 4,096 tokens and packs several documents. Attention is bidirectional among the vision tokens of each image and causal otherwise. It stays within each document in image–text sequences and in every sequence of the text-only reference, whereas the text sequences of image-trained models attend across packed documents. Multimodal training uses a 70:30 mixture of text and image–text sequences, which we select below (table 10). Each image is processed at 224×224224\times 224 resolution and yields 256 vision tokens (section A.1). An image–text sequence packs about 12.8 MetaCLIP 1.2 pairs, each one image and its caption, so vision tokens fill about 80% of an image–text sequence and, under the 70:30 mixture, about 24% of all training tokens. Below, the data ablation varies the mixture and the study of when image–text data enters training uses a 90:10 mixture; the richer patch embeddings of section D.3 read higher-resolution images.

Recaptioning.

Multimodal training uses captions regenerated once for the MetaCLIP 1.2 images by Qwen2.5-VL-32B-Instruct (Bai et al., 2025b) and shared by every recipe, while encoder pretraining uses the original alt-text (section 2). We use nucleus sampling with temperature 0.6 and top-pp 0.95, generating at most 128 new tokens. The system prompt is:

You are an expert image captioner. Write one specific, information-dense caption (1–2 sentences). Do not begin with 'A', 'An', or 'The'. Name the main subject first, then key objects, attributes, actions, and scene context. Avoid hedging and meta phrases.

The user prompt is:

Generate a caption for this image.

Caption source for encoder pretraining.

To ablate the choice of regenerated captions versus alt-text, we pretrain the CapPa encoder for 7.7×10207.7\times 10^{20} FLOPs on either the alt-text or our regenerated captions and train it with the 1B ladder backbone (table 28), a 0.4B encoder, and the 70:30 mixture, against the from-scratch encoder, to 32 and 64 tokens per parameter (table 9). The regenerated-caption encoder scores slightly higher Avg. VQA than the alt-text encoder and matches the from-scratch encoder.

Data mixture.

We select the 70:30 mixture of text and image–text sequences by an ablation on the 1.7B backbone with a from-scratch vision encoder, consistent with controlled studies of data balance in early multimodal training (Han et al., 2026). At the same lifetime compute (2.34×10212.34\times 10^{21} FLOPs, at a constant learning rate), we compare it with 100:0, 90:10, and 50:50 mixtures (table 10). The 70:30 mixture gives the best Avg. VQA with slight degradation to text, whereas 90:10 keeps Avg. Text closer to the text-only model.

We use 70:30 for the main comparisons as it gives a strong balance of visual understanding and language ability.

When image–text data enters.

We also vary the point in training at which image–text data enters. Every schedule allocates 10% of lifetime training examples to image–text data, a 90:10 mixture rather than the constant 70:30 mixture above. We compare schedules that begin image–text training at different points while keeping the total number of image–text examples and lifetime compute fixed (fig. 11). Later schedules continue the language model and optimizer, add a randomly initialized vision encoder and projector, and warm up the new parameters for 4,000 updates. Starting image–text training at the first update gives the strongest visual understanding. Starting at 25%, 50%, or 75% of training lowers Avg. VQA, with the largest drops on general and on OCR and chart questions, while Avg. Text stays comparable (table 11).

\FloatBarrier

A.5 Compute accounting

Lifetime compute (eq. 1) sums the training compute of every stage that produces the final model: multimodal training for every recipe, encoder pretraining for pretrained encoders, and, in midtraining (section 6.2), the text-only pretraining of the language model. As with fine-tuning in transfer evaluation, instruction tuning is a fixed downstream step applied to every checkpoint to measure VQA (appendix B), so it is not counted. Each term uses the same algorithmic count of forward- and backward-pass matrix multiplication and convolution FLOPs for the modules active in that stage (Kaplan et al., 2020; Hoffmann et al., 2022). The count excludes activation recomputation (Chowdhery et al., 2023), optimizer updates, communication, elementwise operations, and input processing. A frozen encoder receives no backward pass during multimodal training, so it is charged only its forward pass, one third of its training cost. The free-encoder comparison of section 6.1 instead matches multimodal training compute and does not charge encoder pretraining.

Charging pretrained checkpoints.

A pretrained encoder is charged the full compute of its upstream training up to the checkpoint used. Because a MetaCLIP example costs less compute than a captioning example, the same upstream compute buys MetaCLIP about 12% more epochs. The objective comparisons hold upstream compute equal across objectives, so they use MetaCLIP checkpoints matched to the compute of 1, 2, 4, and 8 captioning epochs (section C.1). The sweep of section C.3 compares MetaCLIP only with itself, so it uses MetaCLIP’s own 2-, 4-, 8-, and 13-epoch checkpoints.

Token-equivalent budgets.

To provide intuition about compute scales, we also express each budget in token-equivalents, the number of tokens that a text-only model of the same backbone size would train on with the same compute:

Heq=ClifetimecLM,H_{\mathrm{eq}}=\frac{C_{\mathrm{lifetime}}}{c_{\mathrm{LM}}}, (6)

where cLMc_{\mathrm{LM}} is that text-only model’s training FLOPs per token, 1.17×10101.17\times 10^{10} at 1.7B and 2.61×10102.61\times 10^{10} at 4B. For example, a budget of 200B token-equivalents is 2.34×10212.34\times 10^{21} FLOPs at 1.7B, and table 12 gives every decayed budget in FLOPs and tokens per parameter; a constant-learning-rate checkpoint sits at 0.9 times its decayed budget (section A.3).

Architecture and data mixture change the number of updates at fixed compute. For instance, at 2.34×10212.34\times 10^{21} FLOPs, the 1.7B text-only model takes 47.7K updates of 1,024×4,0961{,}024\times 4{,}096 tokens (200B tokens), and the from-scratch encoder recipe with the 70:30 mixture takes 45.3K, because the encoder’s computation also counts toward the budget.

\FloatBarrier

Appendix B Evaluation

This section describes the two main evaluation metrics, Avg. VQA and Avg. Text. We also define the held-out losses that sections 4, 5.4 and F.3 use as well as two additional metrics, out-of-distribution caption loss and ImageNet linear-probe accuracy.

B.1 VQA benchmarks

Visual instruction tuning.

We use instruction tuning as an evaluation protocol (Tong et al., 2024a). Every multimodal model checkpoint is instruction-tuned with one fixed recipe before we measure its visual understanding. The recipe runs three epochs of Cambrian-7M (Tong et al., 2024a) before evaluation. Multimodal training reads 224×224224\times 224 images, but instruction tuning and evaluation raise the resolution to 448×448448\times 448 (1,024 vision tokens), since OCR and chart reading needs fine detail (Tong et al., 2024a; Beyer, 2024). Exhibits whose captions say so instead retain the multimodal-training resolution of 224×224224\times 224 (256 vision tokens), otherwise with the same recipe. The encoder’s learned position table is interpolated to the larger patch grid, and the fixed sine–cosine positions of encoder-free and in-fusion models are recomputed for it. Cambrian-7M is a curated instruction-tuning mixture spanning general visual tasks, OCR and charts, counting, math, science, code, and language-only data. Table 8 provides the optimizer settings and batch size. Instruction tuning updates the same parameters as multimodal training. Therefore, a frozen encoder, e.g., the frozen MetaCLIP encoder in table 16, stays frozen.

Benchmarks and Avg. VQA.

Evaluation follows the Cambrian-1 visual understanding suite (Tong et al., 2024a), using greedy decoding with at most 256 output tokens. Each task is capped at its first 5,000 examples in dataset order. Table 13 lists the 16 benchmarks in four categories (general, knowledge, OCR and chart, and vision-centric), with the split, metric, and number of examples for each. Exact match compares the normalized parsed answer or option letter with the reference answers, relaxed accuracy tolerates small numeric errors, and VQA accuracy is the consensus metric (Antol et al., 2015) that TextVQA uses. Each category mean averages its four benchmarks. The suite contains 15 benchmarks scored in [0,100][0,100] and MME-Perception (MME-P), whose ten subtasks each score out of 200. We divide the MME-P total by 20 to put it on the same scale, and Avg. VQA is the mean of the 16 scores, which equals the mean of the four category means.

Blank-image control.

The blank-image control separates visual understanding from what the question alone supports. It replaces every image with zeros during both instruction tuning and evaluation while keeping the vision-token positions. We use it only for the text-only (100:0) row of the data-mixture ablation (table 10), which has no trained visual pathway. At 1.7B, this row reaches 28 Avg. VQA, a measure of how much the questions alone support (Goyal et al., 2017; Chen et al., 2024; Brown et al., 2026).

B.2 Language benchmarks

Language evaluations use the multimodal checkpoint without instruction tuning. Table 14 lists the 12 benchmarks, their categories, and how each is scored. All tasks rank the answer choices by log-likelihood; MMLU uses five subject-matched demonstrations and averages its 57 subjects equally, and the other tasks are zero-shot. Avg. Text is the mean of the four category scores, each the mean of its benchmarks, with ARC-Easy and ARC-Challenge averaged into one ARC score and RACE-middle and RACE-high combined by test-question count.

B.3 Text-only reference

At the same text-token budget, the multimodal recipes score about as well on Avg. Text as a text-only reference trained on the same text: on average 0.1 point below it at 1.7B and 0.6 below at 4B (fig. 12). The encoder, encoder-free, and in-fusion recipes behave alike. At matched lifetime compute, the reference leads by 0.5 to 3.9 points (table 27), because multimodal training gives 30% of its sequences to image–text data and so sees about 30% fewer text tokens. Vision therefore costs text little beyond the text data it displaces.

B.4 Held-out losses

We measure losses on two kinds of held-out data, both as per-token negative log-likelihood in nats. The held-out text and caption losses score unseen samples of the training distributions, and sections 4, 5.4 and F.3 use them. Out-of-distribution caption loss scores caption sets outside those distributions, and table 25 reports it.

In-distribution.

Held-out text loss is the per-token negative log-likelihood on held-out text from the training text corpus, weighted as in the training mixture. It is scored with the attention masking each model was trained with. Held-out caption loss is the per-token negative log-likelihood of the regenerated captions of MetaCLIP 1.2 images never used in training, so it samples the training caption distribution.

Out-of-distribution.

Out-of-distribution caption loss averages the caption loss of three sets of 5,000 images with equal weight: the COCO validation images with the first of their human reference captions (Lin et al., 2014), MetaCLIP 1.2 pairs with their original alt-text (Xu et al., 2024), and images from a licensed stock-photo collection. It is scored with the attention masking each model was trained with.

B.5 ImageNet linear probes

We use three linear probes on ImageNet-1K (Deng et al., 2009). The downstream probe reads the multimodal model with all weights frozen. It mean-pools the backbone’s final normalized vision-token states and fits an ℓ2\ell_{2}-regularized linear classifier on 50 training images per class. A fixed 10% holdout selects the regularization strength from {10−4,10−3,10−2}\{10^{-4},10^{-3},10^{-2}\}, and the classifier is then refit on all 50,000 images. We report top-1 accuracy on the full validation split. The upstream probe (table 16) fits the same classifier to a frozen pretrained encoder before multimodal training. It mean-pools the encoder’s 256 final normalized patch tokens of a 224×224224\times 224 center crop; for WebSSL, it reads the exponential-moving-average teacher. The full-data probe applies the DINOv2 linear evaluation (Oquab et al., 2024) to the frozen pretrained encoder, training on the full ImageNet-1K training set. It gives the upstream accuracy in fig. 9 and section C.3.

\FloatBarrier

Appendix C Separate encoder pretraining

This section details the pretrained-encoder comparisons of section 3 and the sweep behind the zero-cost pretrained-encoder comparison of section 6.1.

C.1 Objectives and upstream training

We compare four upstream objectives on the same vision encoder architecture (section A.1). MetaCLIP (Xu et al., 2024) uses a symmetric image–text contrastive objective (Radford et al., 2021). If ziz_{i} and wiw_{i} are normalized image and text representations in a batch of size BB, its loss is

ℒclip=−12​B∑i=1B[logexp⁡(zi⊤​wi/τ)∑jexp⁡(zi⊤​wj/τ)+logexp⁡(wi⊤​zi/τ)∑jexp⁡(wi⊤​zj/τ)].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{clip}}=-\frac{1}{2B}\sum_{i=1}^{B}\left[\log\frac{\exp(z_{i}^{\top}w_{i}/\tau)}{\sum_{j}\exp(z_{i}^{\top}w_{j}/\tau)}+\log\frac{\exp(w_{i}^{\top}z_{i}/\tau)}{\sum_{j}\exp(w_{i}^{\top}z_{j}/\tau)}\right]. (7)

Here τ\tau is a learned softmax temperature, initialized at 0.07 and kept at or above 0.01. Cap (Tschannen et al., 2023) uses a causal decoder during upstream pretraining to predict caption tokens from the encoder output fϕ​(x)f_{\phi}(x) (eq. 4),

ℒcap=−𝔼(x,y)​[1|y|​∑jlog⁡p⁡(yj∣fϕ​(x),y<j)].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cap}}=-\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)}\left[\frac{1}{|y|}\sum_{j}\log p(y_{j}\mid f_{\phi}(x),y_{<j})\right]. (8)

CapPa (Tschannen et al., 2023) combines this causal objective with fully masked parallel caption prediction. If ℒpar\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{par}} is the loss that predicts all caption positions in parallel from the image and a fully masked caption input, CapPa’s expected loss is

ℒcappa=0.25​ℒcap+0.75​ℒpar.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cappa}}=0.25\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{cap}}+0.75\,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{par}}. (9)

WebSSL (Fan et al., 2025) follows DINOv2 (Oquab et al., 2024) and combines class-token self-distillation (Caron et al., 2021) and KoLeo regularization (Sablayrolles et al., 2019) with iBOT masked-patch prediction (Zhou et al., 2022),

ℒwebssl=λDINO​ℒDINO+λiBOT​ℒiBOT+λKoLeo​ℒKoLeo.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{webssl}}=\lambda_{\mathrm{DINO}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{DINO}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{iBOT}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{iBOT}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{KoLeo}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{KoLeo}}. (10)

We use the DINOv2 weights λDINO=λiBOT=1\lambda_{\mathrm{DINO}}=\lambda_{\mathrm{iBOT}}=1 and λKoLeo=0.1\lambda_{\mathrm{KoLeo}}=0.1. The DINO term sums over the global and local crops, and the KoLeo term over the two global crops. We discard the text tower, caption decoder, and self-supervised prediction heads before multimodal training. We follow the original objective definitions. MetaCLIP, Cap, and CapPa train on the original alt-text of the MetaCLIP 1.2 image–text pairs, and WebSSL trains on their images alone. Sharing one data source isolates the objective, since the pretraining data alone changes the learned representations (Li et al., 2023a; Fan et al., 2025). Table 15 lists the upstream training settings. MetaCLIP’s text tower is a 12-layer Transformer of width 768 with 12 attention heads over 77 text tokens. The Cap and CapPa decoder follows the published CapPa decoder: 12 layers of width 1,024 with 16 attention heads, a 4,096-wide MLP, and cross-attention to the encoder’s patch tokens in every layer, over captions of up to 64 tokens.

We compare the objectives at matched upstream compute. Each method uses the first checkpoint that reaches the compute of two epochs of the Cap objective over the image–text pairs (1.54×10211.54\times 10^{21} FLOPs). For Cap and CapPa, this is 2 billion image–caption examples. MetaCLIP and WebSSL reach the same compute point after different numbers of examples. Section C.2 uses these checkpoints at both backbone sizes. Section C.2 also uses the first checkpoints that reach the compute of one, four, and eight Cap epochs (0.770.77, 3.083.08, and 6.16×10216.16\times 10^{21} FLOPs), the 7.4%, 30%, and 60% shares of fig. 2. The sweep of section C.3 compares MetaCLIP only with itself, so it uses MetaCLIP’s own epoch checkpoints instead (section A.5).

The ImageNet columns of table 16 give the probe accuracy of each upstream encoder at this matched compute, before multimodal training. MetaCLIP has the highest and WebSSL the lowest top-1 accuracy, yet after multimodal training WebSSL reaches the highest Avg. VQA of the four (section C.2), so their ImageNet recognition ranking does not carry over to Avg. VQA.

\FloatBarrier

C.2 Comparison of encoder objectives

At 1.7B, table 16 compares the from-scratch encoder with encoders pretrained on each of the four objectives and updated during multimodal training, and with a frozen MetaCLIP encoder. The updated pretrained rows are the points at a 15% pretraining share in fig. 2. The from-scratch encoder and WebSSL lead on Avg. VQA, with the other objectives 0.7 to 1.8 points behind, and all updated encoders are comparable on Avg. Text. MetaCLIP serves as the pretrained reference elsewhere because CLIP-style pretraining is the most widely used (section 3), and the from-scratch encoder also matches WebSSL, the strongest objective here. No objective leads every category, as self-supervised WebSSL is best on general and vision-centric questions and the from-scratch encoder on knowledge and on OCR and chart questions. Every pretrained encoder trails the from-scratch encoder on OCR and chart questions, and only WebSSL and Cap gain from their priors, on vision-centric questions. Freezing MetaCLIP gives slightly higher Avg. Text but noticeably lower Avg. VQA, so an encoder that adapts during multimodal training is the stronger choice.

At 4B.

We repeat the comparison on the 4B backbone with three of the objectives, at the 5.8×10215.8\times 10^{21}-FLOP budget of fig. 2 (61 TPP), whose from-scratch and MetaCLIP points are the 4B rows of table 16. WebSSL again scores highest among the objectives and MetaCLIP lowest, on both averages. The from-scratch encoder leads all three on Avg. VQA and Avg. Text, and on every VQA category.

Training trajectories.

Figure 13 follows the from-scratch, updated MetaCLIP, and frozen MetaCLIP encoders through training at the 15% share. Every checkpoint before the last precedes the final learning-rate decay (section A.3), so only the final points match table 16.

Compositional matching.

SugarCrepe pairs each image with a correct caption and a hard negative that replaces, swaps, or adds an object, attribute, or relation (Hsieh et al., 2023). We score the multimodal-training checkpoints before instruction tuning by caption likelihood on over 7,511 items in seven subsets. An item is correct when the correct caption’s summed token loss is lower than the negative’s loss. A control scores the same items with an unrelated image shared by both captions. Within each budget, every recipe reaches a comparable replace-and-swap mean, within about 1.5 points, and differs most on the small object-swap subset (table 17). Unlike VQA (section 4), this readout separates neither encoder-free from the encoders nor pretrained from from-scratch encoders.

C.3 Encoder pretraining at fixed multimodal compute

Figure 9 plots a sweep of experiments that holds multimodal training fixed and does not charge encoder pretraining, unlike the lifetime-budget comparisons of fig. 2. Every model starts from a MetaCLIP checkpoint taken after 2, 4, 8, or 13 epochs over the image–text pairs (section A.5). Every model then receives the same multimodal training: 2.7×10212.7\times 10^{21} FLOPs at 1.7B with the 70:30 mixture. Longer pretraining raises the pretrained encoder’s full-data ImageNet linear-probe accuracy (section B.5) but does not improve Avg. VQA after multimodal training. The shortest pretraining scores highest on Avg. VQA (table 18). A lower encoder learning rate also does not recover a benefit from the encoder pretrained prior. Updating the shortest-pretrained MetaCLIP encoder at a tenth of the shared learning rate gives about the same Avg. VQA and Avg. Text as the full learning rate, and a from-scratch encoder with the same multimodal training matches both (table 18).

Appendix D Dedicated vision capacity

This section describes per-category breakdowns of evaluation metrics and experimental details for section 4.

D.1 Encoder advantage by VQA category

Figure 14 splits the encoder-free deficit compared to the from-scratch encoder by VQA category. The deficit is largest on OCR and chart questions at every budget at both 1.7B and 4B backbone sizes. Avg. Text stays within one point (fig. 3). Appendix I gives every VQA and text benchmark for the runs of each main-text exhibit.

D.2 Encoder-free with increased shared capacity

Parameter-matched encoder-free.

The parameter-matched encoder-free baselines in table 2 give the encoder-free backbone 0.4B extra parameters. The default 1.7B backbone has 28 layers of hidden size 2,048, the wider backbone has hidden size 2,304, the deeper backbone has 36 layers, and the wider and deeper backbone has 30 layers of hidden size 2,176, each with about 2.1B parameters. Table 19 shows how the wider variant does at 4B, using 122-TPP runs of table 27. Compared to the default 4B backbone with 36 layers of hidden size 2,560, the wider backbone has hidden size 2,688 and 4.4B parameters. Here, wider means a larger hidden size, whereas the fixed-token study in table 20 widens only the FFNs and keeps the hidden size at 2,048.

Parameter-matched encoder-free at a fixed token count.

Table 2 matches lifetime compute, so each larger encoder-free variant trains on fewer tokens than the encoder. We therefore also train 1.7B encoder-free backbones with wider FFNs or more layers on the encoder’s token count, which gives each encoder-free variant more compute than the encoder (table 20). We evaluate these runs at a constant learning rate, without a final decay, so we compare rows here only within table 20. At approximately the encoder’s parameter count, added FFN width or depth still leaves the backbone 2–3 Avg. VQA points behind the encoder. Wider or deeper variants both narrow the gap, but wider FFNs need about twice the encoder’s parameters to match it, and the deeper backbone still trails it slightly. Every wider or deeper variant scores higher than the encoder on Avg. Text, consistent with how the shared parameters can also be used by language.

D.3 Richer patch embeddings

The default encoder-free patch embedding is a single linear projection followed by RMSNorm and a learned gate (section A.1). We compare it with two richer patch embedding designs: a normalized two-layer projection inspired by Gemma 4 (Gemma Team, 2026), and a four-layer hierarchical MLP (Touvron et al., 2022) inspired by Inkling (Thinking Machines Lab, 2026a). The lower part of table 21 describes each variant. The normalized two-layer projection changes patch size, resolution, position embeddings, and normalization together. It normalizes each patch with LayerNorm (Ba et al., 2016), projects it linearly, adds learned factorized 2D position embeddings, and then applies LayerNorm, a parameter-free RMSNorm, and a linear map into the backbone. The hierarchical MLP has four linear layers that fold neighboring pixels into channels in stages, with RMSNorm and GELU (Hendrycks and Gimpel, 2016) between them, a final RMSNorm, and no position embedding. In table 21, both richer variants read larger images in larger patches (768×768768\times 768 in 48×4848\times 48 patches and 640×640640\times 640 in 40×4040\times 40 patches, rather than 224×224224\times 224 in 14×1414\times 14 patches), so they produce the same 16×1616\times 16 grid of 256 vision tokens as the encoder. At 5.2×10215.2\times 10^{21} FLOPs, both narrow the gap to the encoder, and the hierarchical MLP matches it on Avg. VQA (table 21). The largest gain is on OCR and chart questions, where the default patch embedding trails the encoder most. Avg. Text is comparable across patch embeddings.

However, when training on 224×224224\times 224 images at 2.6×10212.6\times 10^{21} FLOPs, the two-layer projection gains 1.5 Avg. VQA over the default patch embedding whereas the hierarchical MLP loses 3.1, and both remain far behind the encoder (table 2). The hierarchical MLP helps only when it compresses a higher-resolution image into the same number of tokens. With 224×224224\times 224 instruction tuning, it matches the default patch embedding on 224×224224\times 224 images, while processing 640×640640\times 640 images into the same 256 tokens raises it to 38.8, mostly on OCR and chart questions (24.0 against 10.2). Raising only the instruction-tuning resolution to 448×448448\times 448 quadruples the tokens without compressing them, and the hierarchical MLP then gains 1.4 points, against 4.4 for the default patch embedding. The richer patch embeddings therefore help most with higher-resolution images.

D.4 Comparison with prior work

Prior work, Shukor et al. (2025), find that encoder-free models match or slightly outperform an encoder trained from scratch, whereas we find that the encoder leads (section 4). To investigate this discrepancy, we examine two choices in their setup that may work against the encoder, a reduced encoder learning rate and using the averaged validation loss. We also study a third difference, using alt-text captions rather than regenerated captions. First, we evaluate the runs of the scaling ladder (appendix G) on their averaged loss. We also retrain the ladder’s 0.6B and 1B backbones, sizes within the range of their study, with a reduced encoder learning rate, alt-text captions, or both (table 22). Every other setting matches the ladder’s runs, which serve as baselines.

Encoder learning rate.

Shukor et al. (2025) train their from-scratch encoder at a reduced learning rate, the best of the 0.1×0.1\times, 0.01×0.01\times, and 0.001×0.001\times multipliers they compare. We train the encoder at 0.01×0.01\times the backbone’s peak learning rate, and also at 0.1×0.1\times at 1B, with the projector at the full rate. Instruction tuning trains every encoder at its full rate. We find that lowering the rate shrinks the encoder’s lead (table 22), and most of the drop comes between the full rate and 0.1×0.1\times, whereas their sweep starts at 0.1×0.1\times and never trains the encoder at the full rate. At 0.01×0.01\times, the encoder is comparable to encoder-free on Avg. VQA at 1B and loses its caption-loss lead entirely at 0.6B.

Averaged validation loss.

Shukor et al. (2025) fit their scaling laws to validation loss averaged over interleaved, caption, and text data, with captions that are web alt-text. The text loss does not depend on the image, and in our ladder the interleaved loss barely differs between the encoder and encoder-free. Differences between vision components therefore have a weaker effect on the average, which makes it a noisier signal for comparing them. In our scaling ladder, the averaged loss barely separates the encoder from encoder-free, whereas held-out caption loss separates them clearly and tracks Avg. VQA (fig. 18). At 1.7B and 128 tokens per parameter, the two reach the same averaged loss while the encoder leads by 4.8 Avg. VQA points (fig. 15).

Alt-text captions.

We also train on the images’ original alt-text instead of the regenerated captions, for the encoder and encoder-free alike. This delays the encoder’s lead, as the two tie on alt-text caption loss up to 32 tokens per parameter. With both changes (a 0.01×0.01\times encoder learning rate and alt-text captions), encoder-free reaches a lower alt-text caption loss than the encoder at both sizes and every budget, by 0.04 to 0.07 nats, as Shukor et al. (2025) report. Overall, their finding may reflect an under-trained encoder or an averaged loss that can hide its benefit.

\FloatBarrier

Appendix E In-fusion vision capacity

This section describes the in-fusion vision capacity variants of section 5, which add vision-only modules inside the backbone.

E.1 Implementation and sizing

In each augmented layer, in-fusion (FFN-only) adds a vision-only SwiGLU branch of width FF beside the shared FFN, reading the same normalized input. For backbone width DD and LaL_{a} augmented layers, it adds PFFN=La​(3​D​F+D)P_{\mathrm{FFN}}=L_{a}(3DF+D) parameters. In-fusion also adds zero-initialized vision-only query, key, value, and output projections with the shapes of the shared ones. For HQH_{Q} query heads, HK​VH_{KV} key–value heads, and head dimension dhd_{h}, they add PQKVO=2​La​D​dh​(HQ+HK​V)P_{\mathrm{QKVO}}=2L_{a}Dd_{h}(H_{Q}+H_{KV}) parameters. Attention runs once over the combined projections, so there is no second attention stream. Unless otherwise noted, every allocation augments the first eight layers (La=8L_{a}=8), and table 23 lists the resulting widths and parameter counts.

The depth ablation uses in-fusion (FFN-only) because its branch can be narrowed to fit the budget in any number of layers. Vision-only attention projections have the shapes of the shared ones, so in every layer they would take 0.35B of the 0.4B budget at 1.7B (28 layers) and 0.94B at 4B (36 layers), more than the whole budget.

E.2 Routing, depth, and attention-projection controls

In table 3, shared FFN widening grows the shared FFN of layers 1–8 from width 6,144 to 14,336. The FFN branches have width 8,192 when placed in eight layers and 2,304 when placed in all 28.

Routing at matched compute.

In-fusion (FFN-only) and the separate FFN branch differ only in which tokens use the branch. Because the all-token branch also runs on text tokens, it trains on fewer tokens at matched compute. Routing the branch to vision tokens leads on Avg. VQA at both budgets, while the all-token branch is slightly ahead on Avg. Text (table 24). At the longer budget, routing also raises downstream ImageNet probe accuracy from 61.2 to 66.0 (section B.5). With the same parameters, the separate FFN branch beats shared FFN widening on Avg. VQA (table 3).

Attention-projection controls.

In two 4B contrasts at matched training tokens, the vision-only attention projections improve visual understanding both on their own and alongside an FFN branch (table 25). The first adds only the attention projections of in-fusion to the encoder-free model, and the second compares in-fusion with a model that has only its FFN branch.

E.3 Comparison at longer training

At the longest training budget, 1.11T token-equivalents, in-fusion is comparable to the encoder on both Avg. Text and Avg. VQA at both model scales (table 26). In-fusion (FFN-only) is comparable to the encoder at 1.7B and slightly behind it on Avg. VQA at 4B, where it also trails in-fusion at every budget (fig. 5).

E.4 Where vision tokens are processed

To see where each design processes vision tokens, we probe the 1.7B models at the longest training budget (fig. 16), adapting the probes of Chen et al. (2026). For each backbone block, we measure how much the vision tokens change as one minus the cosine similarity between their hidden state before and after the block, and how much attention caption tokens place on them. In both in-fusion models, vision tokens change mostly in the blocks with vision-only modules and little after them. The encoder-free model keeps changing them through its early and middle shared blocks. The encoder’s tokens enter the backbone already processed, so they change mostly in the first few blocks. After the in-fusion blocks, caption tokens attend to vision tokens more than in the encoder and encoder-free models. The same pattern holds at a fifth of the training budget. These probes suggest that in-fusion capacity performs vision-specific processing in its own early blocks and passes stable vision tokens to the shared backbone, whereas an encoder-free model builds them up across its shared layers.

\FloatBarrier

Appendix F Decay, learning rate, and caption loss

This section lists the evaluation performance of each endpoint (post-decay) of our main comparisons, shows that the shared peak learning rate (section 2.4) does not decide the comparisons, and relates held-out caption loss to Avg. VQA (section 4).

F.1 Decayed endpoints

Table 27 lists the evaluation performance of each recipe’s endpoint at each budget of section 2.4, next to a text-only reference trained to the same lifetime compute. Each endpoint is evaluated after learning rate decay.

F.2 Learning rate

All recipes share one peak learning rate per backbone size, a choice that could bias compute comparisons (Porian et al., 2024). Therefore, at 1.7B backbone size, we repeat the encoder, in-fusion, and encoder-free recipes at half and twice the peak learning rate (encoder-free also at four times), at 39 and 79 TPP (fig. 17). At every learning rate, the encoder leads encoder-free and in-fusion matches or exceeds the encoder. Higher learning rates raise Avg. Text for all three recipes, and have lesser effects on Avg. VQA. The shared learning rate therefore does not decide the visual-understanding comparisons of sections 4 and 5.

F.3 Held-out caption loss

We find that across all four of the recipes, caption loss tracks Avg. VQA along one trend (r=−0.96r=-0.96; fig. 18). By category, OCR and chart questions track it most closely.

Appendix G Scaling ladder

Section 5.4 tests whether the comparisons of sections 4 and 5 hold as the backbone grows, using a ladder of backbone sizes. This section gives the ladder’s setup, the scaling laws fitted to it, and how well the laws predict runs they were not fitted on.

Setup.

The ladder trains the encoder-free, encoder, and in-fusion recipes under the protocol of section 2 on backbones from 0.6B to 6.4B parameters. The backbones follow the architecture of the 1.7B backbone, with query heads of dimension 128 spanning the hidden size, half as many key–value heads, and a feed-forward width three times the hidden size. The vision module grows with the backbone (table 28). The encoder keeps the proportions of the 1.7B pairing: half the backbone’s hidden size dd, one layer fewer than the backbone, an MLP four times its own width, and round⁡(0.75​d/128)\mathrm{round}(0.75\,d/128) attention heads of dimension 128. Its parameter count therefore stays at a nearly fixed ratio to the backbone’s non-embedding parameters. The in-fusion modules occupy the first round⁡(8​L/28)\mathrm{round}(8L/28) of the backbone’s LL layers, 29% of the depth, as at 1.7B. Their widths are set so that they match the encoder’s parameter count.

All recipes at a backbone size share one peak learning rate and one batch size (table 28). The peak learning rate is 3×10−4​1.72×109/Ntot3\times 10^{-4}\sqrt{1.72\times 10^{9}/N_{\mathrm{tot}}}, rounded, where NtotN_{\mathrm{tot}} is the total backbone parameter count. The batch size grows by about 1.5 times per backbone size. Warmup lasts 2 tokens per non-embedding backbone parameter (2 TPP), e.g., 2.8B tokens for the 1.7B backbone, which has 1.4B non-embedding parameters. The other settings follow table 8. The 1.7B and 4B runs of sections 3, 4 and 5 instead keep a batch of 1,024 sequences and 4,000 warmup updates at both sizes. At 1.7B, where the ladder’s batch is also 1,024, each ladder recipe is within two Avg. VQA points of those runs when interpolated to their budgets (sections 4 and 5).

Each recipe and size has one constant-learning-rate run, decayed over the final 10% of training at several budgets (table 29). Each point in figs. 7 and 19 is one decayed endpoint. At 1.7B, the ladder’s encoder is the 0.4B encoder of section 2. At 6.4B, we also train the encoder recipe with the 0.4B encoder of the main runs, to check that this smaller encoder does not limit larger backbones (section A.2). Table 29 lists the downstream scores of every run the laws are fitted on.

Scaling laws.

For Avg. VQA, caption loss, and text loss, we fit a separate law for each recipe. For the losses it takes the form L⁡(N,D)=E+A​N−α+B​D−βL(N,D)=E+A\,N^{-\alpha}+B\,D^{-\beta} (Hoffmann et al., 2022), with NN the non-embedding backbone parameters and DD the token-equivalents (section 2.3), fitted by minimizing a Huber loss on log loss. For Avg. VQA, it is linear in ln⁡N\ln N and ln⁡D\ln D, fitted by least squares. Each is fitted on the recipe’s 17 ladder runs (table 30). From 1.7B to 6.4B, encoder-free needs 2.6 to 3.1 times the encoder’s compute on Avg. VQA, 2.4 to 3.8 times on caption loss, and about the same on text loss. In-fusion needs about the same compute as the encoder on Avg. VQA and text loss, and slightly less on caption loss. Table 31 gives the scaling laws’ errors on every run and on each left-out backbone size. Fitted on the ladder alone, the caption-loss laws also predict the separately trained 1.7B and 4B runs of sections 3, 4 and 5 with an average absolute error of 1.6% (table 32). Their warmup differs from the ladder’s, and at 4B, so do the batch size and the size of the vision module. Figure 19 shows each recipe’s caption-loss law at every backbone size against the runs it is fitted on.

Appendix H Beyond lifetime compute: midtraining and inference

This section describes the full midtraining comparison of section 6.2 and the training and inference speed measurements behind section 6.3.

H.1 Midtraining

Table 33 provides the full midtraining comparison of section 6.2 with per-category metrics. We also show the Avg. VQA of the three main recipes when trained with vision from the start. Each recipe’s schedule lowers the text mixture proportion from 100% to 70% over the first 20B tokens and then maintains the 70:30 mixture. The pretrained MetaCLIP encoder stays frozen for the first 4,000 steps while its new linear projector and the backbone are updated. It then unfreezes with a 2,000-step learning rate warmup. Each midtraining run continues at a constant learning rate to 1.2T token-equivalents and then decays to 1.333T. All midtraining runs use 1.56×10221.56\times 10^{22} FLOPs of lifetime compute, including the backbone’s text-only pretraining but not MetaCLIP’s encoder pretraining. Vision-only parameters exclude an encoder’s linear projection into the backbone and include the patch embedding of the other recipes.

Vision learning rate.

Table 33 uses the same peak learning rate for every parameter. Table 34 instead adjusts the learning rate of the vision path alone, while every other parameter keeps the shared rate. A higher vision learning rate brings the from-scratch encoder to within a point of in-fusion and partially closes MetaCLIP’s gap to the from-scratch encoder, but the from-scratch encoder and in-fusion still lead.

H.2 Training time

Here, we compare the training time of the encoder recipe with encoder-free, in-fusion (FFN-only), and in-fusion. Training time can be compared in two ways: per-step comparisons fix the number of optimizer updates, whereas equal-FLOP comparisons fix total modeled training compute. Because encoder computation counts toward that budget, the encoder recipe completes fewer updates at equal FLOPs, so its equal-FLOP time premium is smaller than its per-step premium.

We measure training time with complete optimizer updates on H200 GPUs with fully sharded data parallelism (FSDP) (Zhao et al., 2023). The matched 4B comparison in table 35 runs the four recipes on 32 GPUs with a global batch of 1,024 sequences. Each row projects training time from measured steady-state update times to the same modeled lifetime compute, 1.04×10221.04\times 10^{22} FLOPs (400B token-equivalents at 4B; section A.5).

Table 35 times the encoder and the in-fusion configurations of table 23, which match the encoder’s 0.4B vision-only parameters, under the 4B training setup above. At equal lifetime compute, neither in-fusion variant measurably changes training time relative to encoder-free. The encoder takes 2.9% longer than encoder-free and 2.6% longer than in-fusion at equal FLOPs. Per step, the encoder takes 5.3% longer than encoder-free. Note that the encoder used here is an unoptimized reference implementation, and encoder-specific optimization can narrow its gap. For instance, a compiled (Ansel et al., 2024) version of the Base encoder in table 5 trains within 0.2% of an in-fusion (FFN-only) model with the same vision-only parameters at 4B.

Encoder pipelining.

Overlapping or pipelining (Huang et al., 2019) the encoder recovers little of its cost. At 4B, running the next microbatch’s encoder forward pass alongside the backbone hides 20–36% of the encoder’s per-step cost. Only the forward pass overlaps, because the encoder’s backward pass waits for the backbone’s gradients. With or without an encoder, a four-stage pipeline has about half the throughput of the encoder recipe under FSDP on the same 32 GPUs. FSDP optimizations applied to the encoder alone, such as prefetching parameters or skipping gradient synchronization between accumulation steps, change step time by less than 0.7%.

Visual workload.

Per step, encoder-free and in-fusion (FFN-only) both train faster than the encoder recipe. Encoder-free saves more because the vision-only FFNs of in-fusion (FFN-only) cost about 95% of the encoder’s FLOPs. In an 8-GPU setup at 1.7B, raising the proportion of image–text data from 10% to 50% widens encoder-free’s saving from 10.0% to 13.2%, while in-fusion (FFN-only) saves 6–7% throughout (fig. 20).

\FloatBarrier

H.3 Inference latency

Section 6.3 compares how fast each recipe serves image requests. We run every design in our own implementation on one H200, so all designs share the same inference code. Each request has one image and 256 text tokens and generates 120 tokens. Largely following the inference benchmark setup of Mono-InternVL (Luo et al., 2025b), we report time to first token (TTFT) and output throughput with 16 concurrent requests and 448-pixel images (1,024 vision tokens) unless noted. Each configuration is measured in four runs, and we report medians with full ranges.

Without a separate encoder, the backbone no longer waits for each image to be encoded, so TTFT falls (fig. 21). In-fusion (FFN-only) still processes every vision token with its vision-only FFNs, and at matched vision-only parameters, it performs approximately the same computation per image as the encoder. Its advantage comes from running in eight wide layers instead of the encoder’s deeper stack of narrower layers (27 at the 0.4B budget), in our eager-mode implementation. The inference time saving grows with resolution, because more vision tokens make the encoder a larger share of the time to first token.

Varying the vision budget.

We also try varying the vision-only parameters across the encoder sizes of section A.2, with both in-fusion variants sized to match each encoder (table 36). In-fusion is faster than the encoder at every budget. The time that vision adds over encoder-free is set by the vision budget rather than the backbone, so in-fusion (FFN-only) saves as much time at 4B as at 1.7B. Its relative inference time saving is smaller at 4B only because the backbone’s own prefill time is longer.
